newsitem.title: USA: Monsanto defends genetic soybean tests.
newsitem.headline: Monsanto defends genetic soybean tests.

text.p: Monsanto Co., which produces genetically altered soybeans, on Wednesday defended the scientific tests that back its safety claims for the crop.
"We did something like 1,800 tests to evaluate those soybeans," Karen Marshall, manager of public affairs for Monsanto, said. "These soybeans are absolutely safe."

The environmental group Greenpeace has continued to protest the genetically altered soybeans and has criticised Monsanto for allegedly not testing the biotech crop for exposure to the herbicide Roundup.

In Frankfurt, Germany, on Wednesday Greenpeace said the European Union's decision to approve imports of products derived from genetically altered soybeans was based on incomplete information and was unsound.

It said data submitted to the EU by Monsanto were based on beans that had not been subjected to Monsanto's own "super weedkiller" Roundup, against which the gene-altering process is intended to protect the plants.
"As such the tests provide no information about the residue of this poison in the plants," Greenpeace's German campaign leader Joerg Naumann told a news conference.

Monsanto's genetically altered Roundup Ready soybeans are resistant to the herbicide, allowing farmers to spray fields to kill weeds without harming the crop. But use of Roundup to kill weeds could result in residue on the harvested soybeans.

Marshall, however, said Roundup residue was not an issue since tolerance levels for the herbicide had been previously established and did not need to be established by testing. So Monsanto's testing focused on genetic alteration.
"What we figured would be the new piece of information was the one protein that we added to the plant itself," she said.

Marshall said Roundup Ready soybeans had been reviewed and approved by regulatory bodies in Argentina, Mexico, Canada Japan, the EU and the United States. She said they had also received food safety approvals in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Denmark.
Merrill Lynch analyst Douglas Groh said that while concerns about the Roundup Ready soybeans must be addressed, he did not expect any impediments to marketing the crops.

"In some form or fashion, Monsanto will be able to commercialize the work that they've done," said Groh, who focuses on agribusiness and biotech companies. He said residue on the soybean crop should not be an issue since Roundup breaks down over time to "environmentally benign" substances.
